A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: SubagentHandback
tools.description:
Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}). The call ends your run, so do everything else first and put everything your caller needs in that one report. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

Only a report delivered through SubagentHandback reaches your caller; plain text you write at the end of your run is NOT delivered. There is no recipient parameter: the report can only go to your caller.

message.description: Your full report for your caller

content.text:
Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- courier:changeset-analyzer: Delegate to this subagent when you need changeset@2 artifacts produced from a git diff. Input is a git diff, optionally a linked spec@1, and optionally smith's criteria_evidence from the TDD run that produced this diff. A diff spanning multiple independent topics produces one changeset@2 per topic, never one bundled entry — see judgment for how topics are distinguished. For each topic, classifies consumer_impact (behavior-change, new-capability, internal-only) and semver_impact (major, minor, patch, none) per shared/references/delivery/changesets.md's decision table, identifies that topic's own changed files, detects breaking changes, and maps acceptance_criteria IDs. Uses smith's criteria_evidence directly when supplied; otherwise reconstructs best-effort file-level evidence from the diff. Summary detail scales with semver_impact — terse for patch/internal-only, full old-to-new-to-required-action detail for major. Output is one or more changeset@2 objects conforming to shared/schemas/changeset@2.json, routed to pr-narrator or release-summarizer. (Tools: All tools)
- courier:commit-analyzer: Delegate to this subagent when the user has staged git changes and needs a conventional commit message written. Input is the staged diff. The agent reads shared/references/delivery/commits.md for type and scope conventions. Output is a JSON object containing commit_message, type (feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore, perf, ci, or build), scope (or null), a breaking flag, and a reasoning scratchpad. The commit message explains why the change was made, not what changed — the diff already shows what changed. The reasoning field is a private scratchpad explaining type and scope selection; it is not forwarded downstream. (Tools: All tools)
- courier:pr-narrator: Delegate to this subagent when the user needs a pull request title and body written for a set of staged or committed changes. Input is a git diff and optionally a linked spec@1 or requirement@1. The agent reads the PR template from shared/references/delivery/github.md and writes from the reviewer's perspective — what does a reviewer with zero prior context need to know to approve this confidently? Output is a JSON object with title, body, labels, and a reasoning scratchpad. The body covers what changed, why it was needed, and how to verify correctness. It explains the change's purpose, not a summary of the diff. Labels are inferred from the change type. (Tools: All tools)
- courier:release-summarizer: Delegate to this subagent when you need a release-artifact@2 generated from a collection of changeset@2 entries. Input is a list of changeset@2 JSON objects, the prior released version string, and a release date in YYYY-MM-DD format. Each input changeset already carries consumer_impact and semver_impact, set at authoring time by changeset-analyzer — this agent does not re-derive them. It filters out consumer_impact: internal-only entries, computes the release version as max(semver_impact) across the remaining changesets applied to the prior version, and carries each changeset's summary through as-is (already written in consumer-facing language at the right detail level). All breaking_changes strings from all input changesets are aggregated into the top-level breaking_changes array. Output is a release-artifact@2 conforming to shared/schemas/release-artifact@2.json. (Tools: All tools)
- courier:review-preprocessor: Delegate to this subagent before a PR is opened, to assemble the complete review package for the reviewer. Input is the changeset diff, optionally a linked spec@1 or requirement@1, test results, and any open questions the author wants answered. The agent bundles these into a structured review package — diff summary, linked spec reference, test result summary, and open questions list — so the reviewer has everything in one place before they start. Mechanical assembly only; no judgment about the change. Output is a JSON object with diff_summary, linked_spec, test_results, open_questions, and a reasoning scratchpad. (Tools: All tools)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- mason:auditor: Delegate to this subagent to audit a plugin directory for ecosystem conformance. Check manifests, declared files, agent structure, prompt-prefix identity, routing, contracts, instruction economy, runtime reference quality, and shared linkage. Use repository validators for deterministic checks. Treat length as a review signal; fail prose only with evidence of filler, repetition, mixed rules, unsupported absolutes, or missing refutation. Read-only. Return a structured report. (Tools: All tools)
- mason:evaluation-adjudicator: Independently compare a completed isolated workflow run with its hidden fixture oracle and live evidence. Return `harness-evaluation@2` without prose scoring. (Tools: All tools)
- mason:evaluation-runner: Run one fixed behavioral fixture in an isolated workspace without reading its answer key. Return `evaluation-run@1` for independent adjudication. (Tools: All tools)
- mason:scaffolder: Delegate when creating a plugin or adding one agent to an existing plugin. Generate conformant manifests, skills, agents, routing, and shared linkage for the requested scope. Copy the constitution byte-for-byte. Return a JSON report of created files. (Tools: All tools)
- mason:schema-designer: Delegate to this subagent when the user wants to design a new JSON Schema for an inter-agent artifact — a structured payload passed between producers and consumers in the plugin ecosystem. Provide a description of what the artifact represents, who produces it, and who consumes it. The designer produces a JSON Schema following ecosystem conventions (draft 2020-12, $id as name@version, all fields documented, reasoning scratchpad field always present, additionalProperties false, required fields listed), checks for conflicts with existing schemas in shared/schemas/, and returns the schema object with a recommended filename. (Tools: All tools)
- muse:auditor: Delegate to this subagent when you need adversarial quality review of a component spec@1 before it enters planning. Input is a spec@1 JSON object describing a UI component. Checks for completeness: missing interactive states (hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty), missing accessibility criteria (role, name, focus order, keyboard operability, live-region or state-announcement behavior), invalid prop combinations not marked as error cases, ambiguous phrasing, scope overlap with other component specs, and unnecessary prose that costs every downstream reader without adding a needed fact. For every issue, produces the rewritten fix, not just a description. Output is a JSON object with an issues array (criterion_id, type, description, suggested_fix) and an overall pass/fail verdict. Standard: can a developer implement this component without one clarifying question? Does not check the spec against source artifacts — that's a verification concern; this checks whether the spec, on its own terms, is complete, unambiguous, and implementable. (Tools: All tools)
- muse:drafter: Delegate to this subagent when you have a completed requirement@1 (or free-text design intent) and need a formal component spec@1 drafted. Input is a requirement@1 and optionally design references (mockup description, existing component family, design-system tokens). Output is a spec@1 conforming to shared/schemas/spec@1.json: id (SPEC-NNN), purpose, scope, non_goals (at least one), acceptance_criteria (at least one), optional api_surface for the component's props. Every criterion must be falsifiable — confirmable by a tester with no implementation knowledge, using only observable behavior: rendered output, focus order, ARIA attributes, emitted events. Props, variants, every interactive state (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty), and accessibility criteria are each named explicitly. Error cases and invalid prop combinations carry is_error_case: true. Unknowns go in non_goals or reasoning — no TBDs anywhere. The muse orchestrator writes the spec to disk after exit-gate passes; this agent returns the spec object only. Also runs in correction mode: given spec_file_path, a criterion_id, and implementer's contradiction report, revises the affected criterion (and any dependent ones) and returns the full corrected spec@1 with revision_note set. (Tools: All tools)
- muse:exit-gate: Delegate to this subagent when a component spec@1 needs a definitive pass/fail judgment before entering the planning phase. Input is a spec@1 JSON object describing a UI component. This is an adversarial gatekeeper — the default disposition is fail, and the spec must earn a pass. The spec passes only if all four conditions hold: every acceptance criterion is a testable proposition with no vague language, no TBDs remain anywhere in the document, error cases and invalid prop combinations are explicitly covered with is_error_case: true criteria, and every interactive state and accessibility criterion (role, name, focus order, keyboard operability) implied by the component's props is present. On fail, every blocker is specific enough for the drafter to make a targeted fix without further clarification. Output is a verdict@1 conforming to shared/schemas/verdict@1.json with artifact_type set to spec@1. This agent is the binding exit gate — its fail verdict halts progression to navigator until the spec is corrected and resubmitted. Maximum 3 retries before escalation to a human reviewer. (Tools: All tools)
- navigator:challenger: Delegate to this subagent when a plan@1 needs adversarial review before implementation. Input is a plan@1 and its source spec@1. Check missing work, dependency order, prescription, batching, error handling, criterion coverage, and interface siblings against live evidence. Return per-issue repairs and a binding pass or fail verdict. (Tools: All tools)
- navigator:estimator: Delegate to this subagent when a plan@1 exists and you need a rough effort estimate before committing to execution. Input is a plan@1 JSON object. The agent produces a per-task time estimate in minutes, marks each task as parallelizable or sequential, lists blocking dependencies by task ID, and produces a total_minutes sum with explicit assumptions. The implementer is assumed to have full codebase context but no domain knowledge of the feature being built. A task is marked parallelizable only if it has no dependency on any other task in the current plan. All assumptions affecting the estimate are listed explicitly in an assumptions array. Output is a JSON object with total_minutes, a tasks array, and assumptions. (Tools: All tools)
- navigator:planner: Delegate to this subagent when you have a completed spec@1 and need a sequenced, executable implementation plan. Input is a spec@1 (or its spec_file_path, read from disk if provided). Output is a plan@1 conforming to shared/schemas/plan@1.json, with spec_file_path and spec_hash propagated from the spec. Decomposes into dependency-ordered tasks (foundational types, then logic, then integration); each task includes exact file paths, a brief implementation approach, exact implementation code as a concrete baseline (smith's implementer may improve on its shape, not its scope), the exact tests proving each criterion it covers, the verification command, a commit message, and covers_criteria naming every acceptance criterion it addresses. Every criterion must appear in some task's covers_criteria. Each task is one independently reviewable unit of change, sized to its Subsystem Batch's compilation boundary rather than a clock-time estimate; no TBDs. Also runs in amend mode: given an existing plan@1, a corrected spec@1, and the changed criterion_ids, patches only the affected tasks (adding new ones for newly introduced criteria) and leaves the rest untouched. Route output to challenger. (Tools: All tools)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- ranger:adversary: Invoke once per candidate after scanner and, for T7 or T10, boundary tracing. Try to refute reachability from current code and return `candidate-assessment@1`. (Tools: All tools)
- ranger:boundary-tracer: Trace T7 and T10 candidates across execution boundaries. Supports Rust, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, and Go. Return `field-survival-map@1`. (Tools: All tools)
- ranger:exit-gate: Independently verify remediated `finding-report@2` entries and their defect families against current code. Return `verdict@3`. (Tools: All tools)
- ranger:recon: Invoke before scanning. Detect affected languages, trace reachable files from live entry points, and inventory project capabilities and current workspace state. Return `workspace-manifest@1`; do not judge defects. (Tools: All tools)
- ranger:scanner: Invoke after recon. Load the hazard pack for each scoped language, scan only live files, and emit every matching `candidate@1` without verdicting. Supports Rust, TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, and Go. (Tools: All tools)
- scribe:arch-auditor: Delegate to this subagent when a draft spec@1 needs checking against the workspace's whole-system architecture before it enters scribe/gate-spec — not against another spec, and not against a single function's signature, but against module boundaries, canonical abstractions, and invariants that span the codebase. Input is a spec@1 draft plus workspace_root. Default (check) mode: reads the persisted arch-model@2 at docs/architecture/model.json (or notes it is absent), reads broadly enough across the workspace to confirm the model still reflects reality, and checks the spec against it — flagging boundary violations (a dependency running the wrong direction), competing abstractions (a new type reinventing something the model already canonicalizes), and invariant conflicts. Output is an arch-audit@1 conforming to shared/schemas/arch-audit@1.json. Build mode: given no usable model or an explicit refresh request, reads the codebase broadly and produces or updates an arch-model@2 conforming to shared/schemas/arch-model@2.json — module boundaries, canonical abstractions, and invariants (each citing its governing decision record when one exists), the latter cumulative across everything scribe/architect has ever fixed. This agent does not patch specs or code — it reports fit, or builds the model fit is checked against. (Tools: All tools)
- scribe:architect: Delegate when `finding-report@2`, `implementation-review@2`, or `implementation-result@1` identifies a structural defect class. Inspect the live semantic model and persisted architecture, then produce a `spec@1` that makes recurrence impossible or machine-detectable. (Tools: All tools)
- scribe:auditor: Delegate to this subagent when you need adversarial quality review of a spec@1 before it enters planning. Input is a spec@1 JSON object. Checks seven dimensions: untestable/vague criteria, ambiguous phrasing, missing error cases, scope overlap with other specs, TBDs/incomplete sections, unnecessary prose that costs every downstream reader without adding a needed fact, and a field this spec introduces or changes on a type that another spec persists, serializes, or transmits with no matching round-trip criterion on the far side and no note that the gap is intentional. For every issue, produces the rewritten fix, not just a description. Output is a JSON object with an issues array (criterion_id, type, description, suggested_fix) and an overall pass/fail verdict. Standard: can a developer implement this spec without one clarifying question? Does not check the spec against source artifacts — that's verifier's role; this checks whether the spec, on its own terms, is complete, unambiguous, and implementable. (Tools: All tools)
- scribe:drafter: Delegate to this subagent when you have a completed requirement@1 and need a formal spec@1 drafted. Input is a requirement@1 and optionally a research-report@1. Output is a spec@1 conforming to shared/schemas/spec@1.json: id (SPEC-NNN), purpose, scope, non_goals (at least one), acceptance_criteria (at least one), optional api_surface. Every criterion must be falsifiable — confirmable by a tester with no implementation knowledge, using only observable behavior. Error cases carry is_error_case: true. Unknowns go in non_goals or reasoning — no TBDs anywhere. The scribe orchestrator writes the spec to disk after exit-gate passes; this agent returns the spec object only. Also runs in correction mode: given spec_file_path, a criterion_id, and implementer's contradiction report, revises the affected criterion (and any dependent ones) and returns the full corrected spec@1 with revision_note set. (Tools: All tools)
- scribe:drift-checker: On-demand diagnostic: given a spec_file_path and a workspace root, verifies the current code still implements every acceptance criterion in the spec. Reads the spec from disk, not from context, and reads implementation/tests from the workspace. When a prior changeset@2's criteria_evidence is available, uses its pointers as a starting point but re-verifies each one — code may have moved since it was recorded. Classifies each criterion as covered (implementation and tests match the contract), uncovered (nothing found), or drifted (behavior diverges from the criterion). Not a blocking gate — exit-gate is. Use for ongoing maintenance, detecting drift weeks or months after implementation. Output is a drift report with covered/uncovered/drifted arrays plus a summary. (Tools: All tools)
- scribe:exit-gate: Issue the binding `verdict@3` for a `spec@1` before planning. Pass only when every criterion is testable, error behavior is explicit, no TBD remains, scope fits one planning cycle, and all checks are complete. (Tools: All tools)
- scribe:verifier: Delegate to this subagent when you need to verify that a draft spec@1 is grounded in its source artifacts — the requirement@1 and optional research-report@1 — before it proceeds to auditing or gating. Input is a spec@1 draft plus the originating requirement@1 and any research-report@1 used to produce it. For each acceptance criterion, the agent checks whether the requirement or research report supplies evidence that the criterion is necessary and correctly scoped. Each criterion is classified as supported (evidence found with a direct citation), unsupported (criterion appears with no basis in the source artifacts), or overfitted (criterion is narrower than the source supports, excluding valid cases). The agent collects evidence only and does not produce a pass/fail verdict. Output is a structured evidence report with supported, unsupported, and overfitted arrays plus a reasoning scratchpad. For post-implementation drift checking, use drift-checker instead. (Tools: All tools)
- sentinel:exit-gate: Issue `verdict@3` from a completed verification report. Separate blockers, coverage gaps, and pending checks; pass only within the verified scope. (Tools: All tools)
- sentinel:recon: Delegate to this subagent at the start of the sentinel gate protocol when an artifact must be inventoried before verification begins. Input is an artifact path or description. The agent determines the artifact type, locates it in the workspace, enumerates the criteria it must be verified against (derived from a linked spec or requirement, or from the artifact's own acceptance criteria section if none is linked), and identifies source files to cross-check during verification. This is purely mechanical discovery — the agent produces no pass/fail opinion. Output is a JSON manifest with artifact_type, artifact_path, criteria array, source_files array, and a reasoning scratchpad. Do not delegate here for judgment; route the manifest to verifier for criterion cross-reference. (Tools: All tools)
- sentinel:verifier: Delegate to this subagent after recon has produced its artifact manifest, and before any final verdict is issued. Input is the recon manifest from recon, including the artifact path, criteria list, and source files. The agent reads the artifact and each source file and, for each criterion, collects concrete evidence that confirms or refutes it. Each criterion is classified as verified (positive evidence found), failed (evidence contradicts the criterion), or unverifiable (requires external context not accessible). Absence of a counter-example is not sufficient to classify a criterion as verified. This agent is a neutral evidence collector — it does not issue verdicts. Output is a JSON object with verified, failed, and unverifiable arrays. Route output to exit-gate for the final verdict. (Tools: All tools)
- smith:exit-gate: Delegate after all planned batches have terminal results and approved `implementation-review@2` artifacts. Verify current code, scoped evidence, sibling completeness, and pending work independently. Return `verdict@3`. (Tools: All tools)
- smith:implementer: Delegate to execute one plan task. Read persisted criteria, design and implement the change, prove it with tests, and record exact evidence. Commit only when the caller supplies `commit_authorized: true`; otherwise return a null commit SHA. Report spec contradictions or architecture needs instead of forcing a pass. Scope is one task. (Tools: All tools)
- smith:mutator: Delegate after implementation. Use available project-native mutation tooling against changed behavior, or a controlled deliberate fault when appropriate. Analyze survivors and return `mutation-report@2`; unavailable tooling becomes a coverage gap. (Tools: All tools)
- smith:recon: Delegate before implementation. Inspect current workspace state, affected languages, entry points, project-native verification capabilities, baseline tests, and persisted artifact freshness. Return `workspace-manifest@1`; stop on a failing baseline. (Tools: All tools)
- smith:reviewer: Delegate after an implementation batch and discrimination check. Review scope, verification fit, related defects, semantic models, and architecture. Return `implementation-review@2`; route structural families to `scribe:architect`. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)
- vanguard:reader: Delegate to this subagent after recon produces a source map. Input is the source map from recon plus the original research question. The agent reads every identified source and extracts findings relevant to the question, with a citation, confidence level (confirmed, likely, or assumed), and source attribution for each. Does not synthesize or recommend — extracts faithfully from what it reads. Sources that cannot be read are noted as unreadable rather than skipped. Output is a JSON object containing a findings array, a sources_read list, and a reasoning scratchpad noting contradictions or surprises. Do not skip any source from the map; recon already filtered for relevance. Route output to synthesizer. (Tools: All tools)
- vanguard:recon: Delegate to this subagent at the start of any research task, before any reading or analysis begins. Input is a requirement@1 or free-text research question. The agent maps where answers might live — existing specs, docs, manifests, codebase patterns, or external sources — and returns a structured research agenda that tells reader exactly which sources to read. Does not read file contents; relevance is assessed from names and directory structure only. Output is a JSON object containing internal_sources, external_keywords, existing_implementations, scope, and a reasoning scratchpad. The source list is intentionally focused: only sources likely to answer the question, not every file in the workspace. Route output to reader. (Tools: All tools)
- vanguard:risk-assessor: Delegate to this subagent when a proposed approach or research-report@1 needs risk review before a spec is written. Input is a proposed approach or research-report@1 JSON, optionally accompanied by context about the target environment. The agent identifies technical risks that would materially affect the spec or plan if left unaddressed. For each risk it produces a description, severity (critical, high, medium, or low), likelihood, a concrete trigger condition describing when the risk materializes, and a mitigation sketch. Only risks with a plausible failure path are included — theoretical concerns without a realistic trigger are excluded. Output is a JSON object with a prioritized risks array and an overall_risk assessment. Surfaces risks neutrally — no recommendation about whether to proceed. (Tools: All tools)
- vanguard:synthesizer: Delegate to this subagent after reader produces a findings list. Input is the findings array and reasoning from reader, along with the original research question. The agent synthesizes findings into a coherent research-report@1, surfaces contradictions between sources, identifies patterns across findings, and lists open questions that remain unanswered. Output is a complete research-report@1 conforming to shared/schemas/research-report@1.json. The recommendation includes an explicit confidence level (high, medium, or low), the rationale, a list of open questions, and any contradictions called out explicitly. Does not resolve contradictions by choosing a side without evidence — accuracy over tidiness. Route output to scribe. (Tools: All tools)
- weaver:auditor: Delegate to this subagent to cross-reference open requirements against existing specs, persisted plans, and implementation files. Input is a list of open requirement@1 objects. Searches for files that address each requirement's done_when criteria — including a persisted plan@1 at docs/projects/ covering the requirement's linked spec, not just a gated spec or shipped implementation — inspects matches for substance, and detects requirements with overlapping or identical core statements. Output is a structured audit report: per-requirement status (covered, partial, missing, duplicate), evidence, duplicate_of references, and a structured summary (per-status counts plus an optional one-clause note). Read-only — modifies nothing. Use before planning to prevent duplicate work. Also runs in a narrower connect mode: given one requirement@1 (or a small set) instead of the full backlog, returns the same per-requirement shape scoped to just what was given. (Tools: All tools)
- weaver:clarifier: Delegate to this subagent when a requirement@1 draft from intake needs review for missing or underspecified dimensions before a spec can be written. Input is a requirement@1 JSON object. The agent evaluates gaps in priority order: testability of done_when criteria, specificity of stakeholder, and explicitness of out_of_scope boundaries. It then either asks one focused clarifying question or, if all dimensions are complete, returns the finished requirement with out_of_scope fully populated. Never asks multiple questions at once — one question per invocation. Output is a JSON object with action (question or complete), question (or null), the current requirement, and reasoning. When action is complete, out_of_scope is populated with explicit scope boundaries. Route completed requirements to drafter. (Tools: All tools)
- weaver:intake: Delegate to this subagent when you have a raw need statement in free text — a problem description, user story, or feature request — and need it converted into a structured requirement@1 draft. Input is unstructured text only; no schema is required from the caller. The agent infers id, statement, stakeholder, why, and done_when from the provided text without asking any clarifying questions. Fields that cannot be inferred are omitted; gaps are noted in the reasoning scratchpad. The out_of_scope field is intentionally left empty — populating it is the clarifier's responsibility. Output is a flat requirement@1 JSON object conforming to shared/schemas/requirement@1.json. Every done_when criterion must be a testable proposition verifiable from outside the implementation. Route this output directly to clarifier before writing a spec. (Tools: All tools)
- weaver:prioritizer: Delegate to this subagent when a set of requirement@1 drafts needs ranking before planning starts. Input is a list of requirement@1 objects. The agent ranks them by impact (who is affected and how badly), urgency (signals in why/done_when indicating time pressure), and dependency order (a requirement that another depends on ranks above the one depending on it, regardless of its own impact/urgency score). Output is an ordered list with a stated rationale per requirement, plus any dependency relationships found. Does not modify requirement@1 objects — ranking and rationale only. (Tools: All tools)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

The official TOON repo reports that TOON matches or slightly beats JSON on accuracy while using about 40% fewer tokens. Independent analysis is more mixed.

- **Official benchmarks:** Results vary by run. One reports 72.2% accuracy (vs JSON's 71.4%) while using 42.6% fewer tokens. Another, on 209 data retrieval questions on 4 models, reports 73.9% accuracy (vs JSON's 69.7%) while using 39.6% fewer tokens.
- **Limits:** The repo says TOON's savings depend on data shape. Deeply nested or non-uniform structures see little tabular benefit, where compact JSON often wins outright. The repo also notes that some deployments, notably local or quantized models, process compact JSON faster despite the higher token count.
- **Independent critique:** A separate analysis of the benchmarks found that TOON ranks 9th out of 12 formats with 47.5% accuracy, performing worse than JSON (52.3%) in that evaluation. The same analysis concluded that TOON demonstrably reduces token usage by 30–60% across multiple studies, but that accuracy results span from strong performance (68.7%) to below-average (47.5%), depending on the evaluation methodology.

Bottom line: the token savings are consistently reported. The accuracy advantage over JSON is small and depends on the dataset, model, and evaluation setup. The official numbers are from the project itself, and the critique is from a third-party write-up, so treat both with some caution.

**Summary:** LocAgent is a framework for code localization, the task of finding where in a codebase changes are needed. It parses a codebase into a directed heterogeneous graph of files, classes, and functions, linked by imports, invocations, and inheritance. LLM agents then use multi-hop reasoning over this graph to locate relevant code from a natural-language issue description.

**Key claims with numbers:**

- **File-level accuracy:** Up to 92.7% on file-level localization, per the abstract's "reaching up to 92.7% accuracy on file-level localization."
- **Cost:** A fine-tuned Qwen-2.5-Coder-Instruct-32B reaches results comparable to state-of-the-art proprietary models at about 86% lower cost ("approximately 86% reduction").
- **Downstream issue resolution:** GitHub issue resolution success improves by 12% at Pass@10 (multiple attempts).
- **Benchmarks:** The abstract reports gains on real-world benchmarks but does not name them or give baseline figures. The full paper would be needed for those details.

content.content:
**Date:** Published November 6, 2025.

**Methodology**
- **Offline evals:** The team used Cursor Context Bench, a dataset of codebase questions with known correct answers. They ran it on the most-used models in Cursor, including their own Composer, with and without semantic search.
- **Online A/B test:** Both groups used the same model. One had semantic search, and the other had only grep-style tools. The test covered all agent queries, not just those that needed search.
- **Training:** The custom embedding model was trained on agent session traces. An LLM ranked which content would have been most helpful at each search step, and the embedding similarity scores were aligned to those rankings.

**Numbers**
- **Accuracy (offline):** Semantic search raised answer accuracy by 12.5% on average, ranging from 6.5% to 23.5% depending on the model.
- **Code retention (A/B):** Retention rose 0.3% overall and 2.6% on codebases with 1,000+ files.
- **Dissatisfied follow-ups (A/B):** Without semantic search, dissatisfied follow-up requests increased by 2.2%.
- **Tokens:** The post reports no token or cost figures.

**Grep vs. semantic search**
- Semantic search improved outcomes for every model tested, with the largest benefit on large codebases.
- Semantic search retrieves code by natural-language meaning (for example, "where do we handle authentication?"). Grep matches text patterns.
- The authors conclude that the best results come from using both. The agent relies heavily on each.

content.content:
**Source:** Cognition blog post, "Introducing SWE-grep and SWE-grep-mini: RL for Multi-Turn, Fast Context Retrieval," dated **October 16, 2025**.

**Models and purpose**
- SWE-grep and SWE-grep-mini are small models specialized in fast, parallel code context retrieval.
- They power "Fast Context," a subagent in Windsurf, and the authors plan to add them to DeepWiki, Devin, and Windsurf Tab.

**Tools**
- A restricted set of tools, including grep, glob search, and file reads, for cross-platform compatibility and safety.
- Up to 8 parallel tool calls per turn.
- Custom-optimized tool execution (indexing, multi-threading).

**Turns and latency**
- Capped at 4 serial turns (3 for exploration, 1 for the answer), versus the 10–20 turns typical of agentic search.
- Raising parallelism from 4 to 8 searches per turn cut search turns from 6 to 4 with similar performance.
- Reported inference speed on Cerebras: SWE-grep-mini above 2,800 tokens/s, SWE-grep above 650 tokens/s.
- Compared with Haiku 4.5 (about 140 tokens/s), that is roughly 20x and 4.5x faster, respectively.
- The authors claim an order-of-magnitude reduction in retrieval time versus frontier models.

**Metrics**
- Weighted F1 (F-β, β=0.5), which favors precision over recall to limit context pollution for the main agent.
- End-to-end latency.
- Exact per-model scores appear only in charts that aren't included in the text provided.

**Training**
- SWE-grep was trained with multi-turn reinforcement learning.
- SWE-grep-mini was distilled from SWE-grep, then given additional RL.
- Reward: average weighted F1 over file retrieval and line retrieval against ground-truth labels.
- Algorithm: a modified policy gradient using per-sequence importance sampling, a leave-one-out baseline, and a maximum token budget during training.
- Stability measures: masking overlong and extreme-ratio trajectories, removing format rewards, zeroing malformed tool calls, and scaling advantages by average tool calls per turn.

**Evaluation**
- Internal "Cognition CodeSearch Eval," built from real repositories, user queries, and labeled relevant files and line ranges.
- Downstream coding: a subset of difficult SWE-Bench Verified tasks run in Windsurf Cascade with Sonnet 4.5 as the main model. The same number of tasks finished in significantly lower end-to-end time.
- Codebase Q&A: latency compared against Claude Code and Cursor CLI on open-source repositories.

**Comparisons**

**Source:** Cognition blog post, "Introducing SWE-grep and SWE-grep-mini: RL for Multi-Turn, Fast Context Retrieval," dated **October 16, 2025**.

- SWE-grep and SWE-grep-mini are small models specialized in fast, parallel code context retrieval.

- A restricted set of tools, including grep, glob search, and file reads, for cross-platform compatibility and safety.
- Up to 8 parallel tool calls per turn.
- Custom-optimized tool execution (indexing, multi-threading).

**Turns and latency**
- Capped at 4 serial turns (3 for exploration, 1 for the answer), versus the 10–20 turns typical of agentic search.
- Raising parallelism from 4 to 8 searches per turn cut search turns from 6 to 4 with similar performance.
- Reported inference speed on Cerebras: SWE-grep-mini above 2,800 tokens/s, SWE-grep above 650 tokens/s.
- Compared with Haiku 4.5 (about 140 tokens/s), that is roughly 20x and 4.5x faster, respectively.
- The authors claim an order-of-magnitude reduction in retrieval time versus frontier models.

- Weighted F1 (F-β, β=0.5), which favors precision over recall to limit context pollution for the main agent.
- End-to-end latency.

- SWE-grep was trained with multi-turn reinforcement learning.

- Algorithm: a modified policy gradient using per-sequence importance sampling, a leave-one-out baseline, and a maximum token budget during training.

content.content:
**Models and setup**
- Four models were tested: claude-haiku-4-5, gemini-3.6-flash, gpt-5.4-nano, and grok-4.5.
- Six formats were compared: TOON, JSON, XML, YAML, compact JSON, and CSV.
- The run used 244 retrieval questions, for 5,856 LLM calls. Reasoning was disabled, and temperature was left at each model's default.
- Token counts use the `o200k_base` tokenizer. The README notes that other providers tokenize differently.

**Datasets**
- The catalog has 13 datasets, from 1-row deeply nested configuration to 100-row uniform employee records.
- Structure classes are uniform, semi-uniform, nested, and deep. Tabular eligibility ranges from 0% to 100%.
- Four validation datasets test truncated arrays, extra rows, missing fields, and inconsistent field counts.

**Accuracy (all 244 questions)**
- TOON scored 72.2%, JSON 71.4%, YAML 70.1%, XML 70.7%, and compact JSON 69.0%. CSV was excluded because it only covers flat data.
- TOON used about 2,474 tokens on average, versus 4,308 for JSON.
- On the 109 flat-dataset questions, TOON (63.1%) and CSV (62.2%) led, and the margin was within the reported confidence intervals.
- Per model, TOON was ahead of JSON on Haiku, Gemini, and Grok, but it ranked third on gpt-5.4-nano, behind XML and JSON. Many gaps overlap the Wilson 95% intervals, so the README treats them as not statistically meaningful.

**Token counts**
- Mixed-structure track: TOON totaled 264,734 tokens, versus 393,637 for JSON (−32.7%), 314,140 for YAML (−15.7%), and 447,936 for XML (−40.9%). Compact JSON was slightly smaller than TOON on this track (TOON was +1.6% against it).
- Flat track: TOON totaled 68,030 tokens, about 5.9% above CSV's 64,247, but about 58.7% below JSON.

**Stated limitations**
- CSV can't represent nested data without lossy flattening, so it's left out of the mixed track and the efficiency ranking.
- Absolute token counts are specific to this tokenizer. The README says relative differences "hold directionally."
- Per-model CSV results cover a smaller, easier question set.
- Latency wasn't measured. The README says it's "the one you have to measure yourself," and notes that compact JSON can run faster on some local or quantized setups.

**When not to use TOON (per the README)**
- Deeply nested or non-uniform data, where compact JSON often wins.
- Semi-uniform arrays (about 40–60% eligibility), where savings shrink.
- Purely tabular data, where CSV is smaller. TOON's roughly 5–10% overhead buys declared lengths and field lists.
- Latency-sensitive deployments, where measurement on your own setup is needed.

Ripgrep 15 is a 2025 major release, with 15.1.0 and 15.2.0 following in 2026. The search didn't return the full 15.1.0 changelog.

- **15.0.0 (October 2025):** Its release notes describe a major version that mostly has bug fixes, some minor performance improvements and minor new features. Notable changes include ripgrep respecting jj's gitignores, support for nested curly braces in globs (globset crate now support nested alternates), and ripgrep binaries compiled with full LTO enabled. On the platform side, aarch64 for Windows now has release artifacts, while powerpc64 no longer has release artifacts generated for it. The release also removed ripgrep's simd-accel feature because it was frequently broken.

- **15.2.0 (July, year not stated in the snippet):** Its notes say it fixes a number of bugs related to gitignore matching as well as some performance improvements in directory tree traversal. It also adds aarch64-unknown-linux-musl to the release binaries and fixes a bug with how ripgrep handles line buffering.

The official changelog on the GitHub releases page is the authoritative source for full details.

The search turned up several 2026 benchmarks, but little on Sweep specifically and nothing direct on Augment or Aider beyond what's below.

**Grep vs. embeddings**
- Coding agents are split. Claude Code and Codex CLI ship without a semantic index, while Cursor and GitHub Copilot use embeddings. Cursor measured that adding semantic search to grep gave 12.5% higher accuracy on its own question-answering benchmark and 2.6% more code kept on codebases over 1,000 files.
- A May 2026 study found that Grep returned in the agent's context beat vector retrieval for every harness and model, but delivering results through files or the vendors' CLIs could "invert or erase the lexical advantage".
- CORE-Bench (June 2026, arXiv 2606.11864) reports "a sharp drop from traditional code search to code retrieval in agentic coding settings" for embedding models.
- Agent Retrieval Bench (arXiv 2607.24882, July 2026) covers 427 samples across 25 repositories and evaluates lexical retrieval, RepoMap, and open-source embeddings. In its results, 0.0841 for Grep strict, 0.1102 for RepoMap, and 0.1247 for Qwen3-4B appear as scores on its final F1 metric. The paper also says its scripted grep diagnostic is not a realistic agent or an estimate of grep's capability., so treat that comparison cautiously.

**Structural and repo-map retrieval**
- Sourcegraph's benchmarks, as reported by a secondary blog, show that baseline grep-and-read retrieval scored file recall of 0.127 and precision@5 of 0.140; swapping in code-intelligent retrieval, a symbol's actual definition plus its call sites, lifted file recall to 0.277 and precision@5 to 0.478. I could not verify this against Sourcegraph's own publication.
- In Agent Retrieval Bench, an aider-style RepoMap was the best model on the trace2code task (MRR 0.2742).

**Tool landscape**
- Augment Code uses a hosted index (Context Engine), and Cursor and Claude Code use agentic grep with no index. If the consumer is a coding agent, use the agentic grep built into Claude Code or Cursor. This is a vendor comparison page, so weigh it accordingly.
- One practitioner guide suggests trying repo-map first and reaching for embeddings last, and notes that embeddings are expensive. Its source is an individual blog, not a benchmark.

**Gaps:** I found nothing on Sweep's retrieval approach, and no direct 2026 benchmark for Augment's Context Engine or Aider's repo map beyond the Agent Retrieval Bench entry above.

- **Response format:** Offer a `response_format` parameter, such as a `"concise"` or `"detailed"` enum, so the agent can choose verbosity. In the article's example, the concise response used about a third of the tokens.

- **Structure:** XML, JSON, or Markdown can all affect performance, so pick the format that scores best in your own evaluations.
- **Token limits:** Use pagination, range selection, filtering, and truncation with sensible defaults. "we restrict tool responses to 25,000 tokens by default" is the article's Claude Code example.
- **Steering truncated results:** When truncating, include instructions that push agents toward efficient strategies, such as many small, targeted searches instead of one broad search.
- **Error messages:** Make them specific and actionable, with examples of correctly formatted input, rather than opaque codes or tracebacks.
- **Namespacing:** Group tools under service and resource prefixes (e.g., `asana_search`, `asana_projects_search`) to reduce confusion. Prefix versus suffix choice affects results, so test it.

content.content:
**Summary:** Agent Retrieval Bench is a file-level benchmark for the retrieval step that comes before a coding agent writes a patch. It has 427 samples across 25 repositories, split into 345 positive examples, 50 natural no-gold examples, and 32 counterfactual wrong-repository controls. The corpus includes 308 base-commit snapshots, 392,000 files, and 7.9 million chunks.

**Retrieval methods compared:** lexical retrieval, RepoMap, open-source embedding models, selective abstention (declining to retrieve when no file is relevant), and logged agent context selection.

**Key findings:**
- **No single method wins everywhere.** "No single retrieval family dominates" is the paper's own framing. Qwen3-Embedding-4B has the best sample-weighted MRR on positive samples, Qwen3-Embedding-8B has the best Recall@20, and RepoMap gives the best budgeted context yield at 8K tokens. Winners also differ substantially by task.
- **Selective abstention is poorly calibrated.** Thresholds calibrated with counterfactual controls did not improve selective success on natural no-gold cases.
- **Agent trajectories miss context.** Logged agent trajectories missed every gold file on 27–35% of samples.
- **Starting context helps.** In a seed-intervention pilot, retrieval-derived initial context gave higher file F1 and less post-seed exploration than random non-gold context. Oracle gold context showed substantial remaining headroom.

**Grep vs. embeddings vs. RepoMap:** The abstract doesn't mention grep specifically, so the closest comparison is lexical retrieval, and its numbers aren't given in the abstract. Based on the abstract, embeddings (especially Qwen3-Embedding models) lead on ranking metrics (MRR, Recall@20), while RepoMap leads on budgeted context yield at 8K tokens. The paper does not identify one clear winner, so the right choice likely depends on the task and context budget. The full paper would be needed for lexical results and detailed per-task comparisons.

**Performance**
- Helper binaries are no longer looked up on Windows unless `-z/--search-zip` is used.
- Hyperlink emission on Windows skips path canonicalization.
- Large `-A/--after-context` values run faster.
- Release binaries use full LTO, giving small speedups and a slightly smaller binary.

**Features**
- `-r/--replace` now works with `--json`.
- Some Jujutsu (`jj`) repositories are treated as git repositories, so ripgrep respects their gitignores.
- Globs support nested curly braces.
- Windows `aarch64` release artifacts are now published.
- `--color` accepts `italic` as a style attribute.
- A new `highlight` color type styles the non-matching text within a matching line.
- Fish completions account for the config file.
- Hyperlink-format completions are improved for bash, fish, and zsh.
- With multithreading, files are searched in the order given on the command line.
- The default file type definitions were expanded.
- `powerpc64` release artifacts were dropped because the CI workflow broke.

- Several gitignore bugs were fixed, including rules inherited from parent directories, whitelisted hidden files, absolute paths with global gitignores.
- `rg -vf` with an empty pattern file now matches everything.
- A UTF-8 byte order mark at the start of `.gitignore` files is ignored.
- Memory usage was reduced for very large gitignore files.
- `--stats` could report an incorrect "bytes searched" value.
- Globs ending in `.` are handled correctly.
- `-m/--max-count` combined with `-U/--multiline` no longer shows too many matches.
- `-r/--replace` preserves line terminators.
- `-q --files-without-match` no longer inverts the exit code.
- Documentation now notes the difference between `-c/--count` and `--files-with-matches`.
- Summary statistics are correct with `--json`.
- A rare panic with certain large regexes on large inputs is fixed.
- A panic when combining `-U/--multiline` and `-r/--replace` is fixed.
- Hyphens in flag names are escaped correctly in the man page.
- macOS `aarch64` builds statically compile PCRE2.

A Measurement Methodology and Preliminary Study","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.13568"},{"title":"SpIDER: Spatially Informed Dense Embedding Retrieval for Software Issue Localization","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.16956"},{"title":"Why grep Is Beating Your Vector DB","url":"https://www.shaped.ai/blog/why-grep-is-beating-your-vector-db"}]

The main match is the arXiv paper "Is Grep All You Need? How Agent Harnesses Reshape Agentic Search" (arXiv:2605.15184), which a DEV Community write-up dates to May 14, 2026. Its headline finding is that grep beats vector retrieval under inline tool delivery, but the advantage depends on the harness.

- **Core result:** Across its harnesses, grep led in every inline-delivery pairing. With inline delivery, lexical search is uniformly stronger than dense retrieval: inline grep exceeds inline vector for every harness–model pair.
- **Harness effects:** The lead does not survive every setup. File-based delivery rearranges the comparison: vector scores higher in five of the ten pairs. The authors conclude that file-based delivery and provider CLI shells able to invert or erase the lexical advantage without any change to the corpus.
- **Scope:** The authors say they do not claim grep is generally better. They claim only that it can win end-to-end under the task distribution and corpora they study. The experiments use 116 LongMemEval questions on conversational memory, not code repositories. A later paper (arXiv 2608.01507) makes the same point, noting that the grep study studies conversational memory rather than code repositories.
- **Code-specific evidence:** A separate paper (arXiv 2608.13568) finds that a language server helps mainly where grep is noisy. Whether semantic retrieval helps a reference-finding task is governed by the symbol's naming collision rate, not by the language.
- **Attribution:** One aggregator page credits PricewaterhouseCoopers researchers with the paper. I did not confirm that against the arXiv listing.

**Abstract summary:** The paper asks whether Language Server Protocol (LSP) retrieval saves tokens for coding agents compared with grep, at equal task success. It defines one metric, tokens-to-success, and runs a five-arm ablation on Python and TypeScript repos with Claude Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6, and Haiku 4.5. The author concludes the answer is "conditional and usually negative."

**Key findings:**

- **Localization by symbol name:** LSP increases token use by 6% to 118%. Agents also ignore it when it is free.
- **Reference completeness:** LSP improves precision but does not save tokens. It cannot raise the recall ceiling set by agent thoroughness. It saves tokens only for the weakest model, Haiku 4.5.
- **Tool choice:** Models default to grep for localization, using semantic tools 0% to 6% of the time. On reference tasks, they use LSP about half the time without being prompted.
- **Multi-file renames (scored by test execution):** Grep solves them perfectly. A location-only LSP fails about three-quarters of them by missing a call site.
- **Text-enriched LSP:** Even with indexing warmed and each reference's line included, LSP recovers most of the gap but cannot close it. Renames must also touch comments and strings, which semantic references exclude.

**Implication:** The author argues against using LSP everywhere. Instead, an adaptive router should choose a tool based on task class, model capability, and lexical noise.

content.content:
**Overview:** The paper (arXiv:2608.01507, submitted Aug 2, 2026, under review at a journal) compares two ways code agents locate code in a repository, using the SWE-QA benchmark for repository-level code question answering.

**Approaches compared**
- **Semantic Search:** The agent retrieves code from a vector index built in advance.
- **Deep Agentic Search:** A planning agent hands exploration to a subagent with its own context window, which returns a condensed result. The paper also calls this "grep-search by subagent."

**Key findings**
- **Accuracy:** Semantic Search answered 65.2% of questions correctly. Deep Agentic Search answered 46.2% correctly.
- **Cost:** Semantic Search produced each correct answer at less than half the cost of Deep Agentic Search.
- **Failure modes:** Deep Agentic Search did not eliminate failures. It added a new class of them. The largest share of its failures, 41.8%, occurred at the planner-to-subagent handoff. These were usually silent, ending in a confident but wrong answer.
- **Conclusion:** The authors argue that the context protection Deep Agentic Search provides is not free. For read-only questions over a repository that can be indexed, retrieval was the stronger and cheaper option.

**Gaps in the source**
- The page gives no absolute token counts or dollar figures, only the relative "less than half" cost claim.
- It does not break down which specific retrieval tools or configurations drove the results beyond the two approaches above.

**Architecture:** Type-aware linting uses two binaries. The Rust-based `oxlint` CLI handles file traversal, ignore logic, diagnostics, non-type-aware rules, and JS plugins. It passes paths and configuration to `tsgolint`, a Go binary that runs the type-aware rules and returns structured diagnostics.

**Rule count:** `tsgolint` plus `oxlint` supports 43 type-aware rules. The post notes that 59 type-aware rules exist in `typescript-eslint`, so coverage is 43 of 59.

**Performance vs. ESLint:** The post's benchmarks (MacBook Pro M2 Max, 12 cores) show:
- **vuejs/core:** 2.531 s (Oxlint) vs. 20.800 s (ESLint + typescript-eslint), an 8.22x improvement.
- **outline/outline:** 4.448 s vs. 55.070 s, a 12.38x improvement.

The post summarizes this as "around 10 times faster." It also says the benchmarks are in a public repository, which I haven't checked.

**TypeScript dependency (tsgo):** `tsgolint` is built on `typescript-go`, Microsoft's Go rewrite that is slated to become TypeScript 7.0. It doesn't use typescript-go's public APIs. It shims internal APIs instead, and the fork is kept current with Renovate. The post says that after TypeScript 7.0's official release, the project will track stable releases rather than the main branch. Because of this, pre-7.0 syntax and deprecated tsconfig options such as `baseUrl` are not supported.

Note that this is the alpha announcement. The page says type-aware linting has since reached stable, so the stable release post is the current reference.

**Scope note.** I ran about 12 searches and 12 fetches. Items marked VERIFIED were read at the primary URL (WebFetch returns a model summary of the page, not raw text). Items marked SNIPPET came only from search results. I did not cover ast-grep, SCIP/scip-typescript, Glean, Semgrep, Zoekt/Amp, Augment, Sweep, Aider, Continue or Cline, MCP size limits beyond one data point, RRF or BM25F sources, or memmap and regex-automata. Several 2026 arXiv IDs came from search results, and I only read their abstract pages.

## Sources

### 1. Agent code-finding: grep vs semantic vs hybrid

- **Cursor, "Improving agent with semantic search"**, cursor.com/blog/semsearch, 2025-11-06. VERIFIED.
  - Offline, on Cursor's own Context Bench with known answers, semantic search on top of grep raised answer accuracy by 12.5% on average (6.5% to 23.5% depending on model).
  - Online A/B, same model: code retention rose 0.3% overall and 2.6% on codebases of 1,000+ files. Dissatisfied follow-ups rose 2.2% without semantic search.
  - The embedding model was trained on agent session traces, with an LLM ranking which content would have helped.
  - Conclusion: grep plus semantic search together is best. No token or cost figures are given. It is vendor data on an internal benchmark.
- **Cognition, "Introducing SWE-grep and SWE-grep-mini"**, cognition.com/blog/swe-grep, 2025-10-16. VERIFIED.
  - Tools are restricted to grep, glob and read, with up to 8 parallel calls per turn and at most 4 serial turns (versus 10 to 20 typical).
  - Trained with RL on weighted F-beta (beta=0.5, precision-favoring) over files and line ranges. The reason given is to avoid polluting the main agent's context.
  - Claims 2,800+ tokens/s on Cerebras (about 20x Haiku 4.5) and matching frontier-model retrieval at far lower latency.
  - They say the head-to-head is "not a rigorous benchmark". The eval is internal and exact scores are only in charts.
- **"Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code QA"**, arXiv 2608.01507, 2026-08-02. VERIFIED (abstract).
  - On SWE-QA, a prebuilt vector index answered 65.2% of questions correctly versus 46.2% for subagent grep exploration.
  - The index approach cost less than half as much per correct answer.
  - 41.8% of subagent failures were silent planner-to-subagent handoff errors.
  - This contradicts the "grep is all you need" narrative for read-only Q&A. It is a single benchmark under journal review.
- **"Is Grep All You Need? How Agent Harnesses Reshape Agentic Search"**, arXiv 2605.15184, May 2026. Abstract only.
  - Inline grep beat inline vector retrieval for every harness and model pair. With file-based delivery, vector won in 5 of 10 pairs.
  - It uses 116 LongMemEval conversational-memory questions, not code, so it is weak evidence for code.
- **Agent Retrieval Bench**, arXiv 2607.24882, July 2026. VERIFIED (abstract).
  - 427 samples across 25 repos.
  - No single method wins. Qwen3-Embedding-4B has the best MRR, 8B has the best Recall@20, and an Aider-style RepoMap gives the best yield at an 8K-token budget.
  - Logged agent trajectories missed every gold file on 27 to 35% of samples.
  - Seeding the agent with retrieval-derived initial context gave higher file F1 and less exploration.
  - Selective abstention was poorly calibrated.
  - SNIPPET only: its scripted grep scored strict F1 0.0841 versus 0.1102 for RepoMap. The paper itself says the scripted grep is not a realistic agent.
- **"Does a Language Server Save Tokens for Coding Agents?"**, arXiv 2608.13568, 2026. VERIFIED (abstract).
  - Python and TypeScript, Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.6 and Haiku 4.5.
  - For localization by symbol name, LSP increased tokens by 6% to 118%.
  - Models chose semantic tools 0 to 6% of the time for localization and defaulted to grep. They used LSP about half the time for reference tasks.
  - Multi-file renames: grep solved them perfectly, and location-only LSP failed about 75% of them by missing call sites.
  - Renames must touch comments and strings, which semantic references exclude. This is relevant to the planned `dependents` command.
  - Its conclusion is that structured tools help where grep is noisy (high symbol-name collision rate), and that an adaptive router is needed.
- **Anthropic and Boris Cherny on Claude Code dropping a local vector DB for glob/grep/read.** SNIPPET only, from secondary blogs. I could not verify the primary quote.
- **Sourcegraph code-intelligence retrieval** (file recall 0.127 to 0.277, P@5 0.140 to 0.478). SNIPPET only, from a secondary blog. Could not verify.

### 2. Localization research and output shape

- **LocAgent**, arXiv 2503.09089. VERIFIED (abstract only).
  - A directed graph of files, classes and functions linked by imports, calls and inheritance, with LLM multi-hop traversal.
  - Up to 92.7% file-level accuracy and an 86% cost reduction with a fine-tuned 32B model. GitHub issue resolution up 12% at Pass@10.
  - SNIPPET only: an independent benchmark (arXiv 2509.25242) reports LocAgent at roughly 35% file-level Acc@5 on non-code or mixed issues. Treat the 92.7% as benchmark-specific.
- **SWE-agent ACI**, arXiv 2405.15793. VERIFIED (abstract). It argues agents need purpose-built interfaces. The abstract gives no design numbers.
- **Anthropic, "Writing tools for agents"**, anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents. VERIFIED.
  - Offer a concise/detailed `response_format` (concise was about a third of the tokens in their example).
  - Return high-signal fields and drop opaque IDs.
  - Claude Code caps tool responses at 25,000 tokens by default.
  - Truncation messages should steer toward narrower searches.
  - Errors should be specific and actionable, with a corrected-input example.
  - Pick the output format by running your own evals.
- Not read: RepoGraph, CodeRAG-Bench, Agentless.

### 3. Structural tooling

- **Oxlint type-aware alpha**, oxc.rs/blog/2025-12-08-type-aware-alpha. VERIFIED.
  - oxlint (Rust) calls tsgolint (Go, built on typescript-go via shimmed internal APIs). 43 of 59 typescript-eslint type-aware rules.
  - 8.2x to 12.4x faster than ESLint on their own benchmarks.
- **TypeScript 7.0 (native Go port).** SNIPPET only, from several blogs. GA about 2026-07-08, with `tsc` now the native binary. The old Strada JS API is not supported, so programmatic use waits for 7.1 or dual installs. The "8 to 12x" build speedups are vendor-reported.
- **Not verified:** the VoidZero acquisition by Cloudflare (2026-06-04) came from a single French blog. I found nothing on scip-typescript, ast-grep or Glean.

### 4. Token-efficient output

- **TOON repo benchmarks**, github.com/toon-format/toon. VERIFIED.
  - 244 questions, 4 models, 6 formats. Accuracy: TOON 72.2%, JSON 71.4%, compact JSON 69.0%. Tokens: about 2,474 for TOON versus 4,308 for JSON on average.
  - The README admits most accuracy gaps are inside the confidence intervals. Compact JSON is slightly smaller on mixed or nested data, and CSV is about 6% smaller on flat data. Latency was not measured.
  - The README itself says TOON is a poor fit for non-uniform data.
  - SNIPPET only: one third-party critique (dev.to) ranked TOON 9th of 12 formats at 47.5% versus JSON at 52.3%. Could not verify.
- The 25K-token cap is verified above under Anthropic. I did not find MCP spec limits.

### 5. Ranking

- **Not verified, no primary source read.** The only item was SNIPPET-level, from crate docs: emit each identifier's subtokens plus the whole identifier, and handle acronym runs (`HTTPSConnection` becomes `https connection`). I found no study on RRF k=60 or BM25F. The k=60 default is from the original Cormack et al. paper, from my own background knowledge, not checked here.
- **Weak evidence only:** Agent Retrieval Bench found lexical, RepoMap and embedding methods each win on different tasks.

### 6. Rust and CLI

- **ripgrep 15.0.0 release notes**, github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/releases/tag/15.0.0, October 2025. VERIFIED.
  - Full LTO release binaries, nested-brace globs, jj repos treated as git repos for gitignore, several gitignore bug fixes, reduced memory on huge gitignores.
  - `--replace` now works with `--json`, files searched in command-line order under multithreading, and `simd-accel` removed.
  - SNIPPET only: 15.1.0 (about May 2026) and 15.2.0 (gitignore fixes, traversal performance, aarch64 musl).
- Nothing on cargo-dist, memmap or regex-automata.

## Implications for monokl (prioritized)

1. **Return code, not only names.** Emit a ranked file:line hit with 1 to 3 lines of matched context, grouped by symbol. The evidence is Cognition's line-range F1 reward, Anthropic's "high-signal fields" guidance, and the LSP paper's finding that "text-enriched" results recover most of the gap. Our eval's 6x token loss to ripgrep likely comes from agents having to re-read after a name-only result. Hard evidence on snippet versus no-snippet shape is thin, so test it in our own eval.
2. **Add a text fallback over all content.** Index or scan comments, string literals, calls, routes, config and tests, not just top-level declarations. The LSP paper shows renames and literals need text matching, and Cursor and Cognition both keep grep as a core tool. Implement via `ignore` plus `grep-searcher` for a residual lexical pass, with no persistent index (consistent with PRINCIPLES). Treat declaration BM25 as a boosting signal, not the sole index.
3. **Never return silent empties.** Return a structured message with the count scanned, which terms matched zero, near-miss identifiers and a next-step hint. Evidence: Anthropic's actionable-error guidance and Agent Retrieval Bench's finding that abstention is poorly calibrated, which argues for hints over silence.
4. **Rank members above containers (or collapse them).** Score at member level and attach the parent as context. A class should not outrank the method that matches. This rests on our own eval plus Cognition's precision-favoring F-beta. No source tests it directly.
5. **Expose a concise/detailed mode and an explicit budget.** Default concise, with counts like `items_returned`/`items_total` and a truncation note that steers toward narrower queries (Anthropic, including the 25K cap). Keep it well below that cap.
6. **Make compact JSON or a plain table the default, with TOON optional.** TOON's own README shows its gains are 5 to 10% in flat cases and negative against compact JSON on nested ones. Agent-facing hits with context are not uniform tables. Benchmark on our eval before committing.
7. **Tokenize identifiers into subtokens plus the whole identifier**, with acronym handling, and index path tokens. Evidence is weak (crate practice only). Verify it ourselves with an ablation.
8. **Provide a RepoMap-style summary mode** (outline of files and exported symbols within a token budget). It was the best performer at an 8K budget in Agent Retrieval Bench, and it plays to our declaration-only strength.
9. **Keep OXC.** The TS 7 native port removes the JS compiler API but not syntactic parsing. Avoid depending on type information. If type-aware features are ever needed, the oxlint/tsgolint pattern (spawn a Go binary) is the precedent.
10. **Defer embeddings.** Cursor's +12.5% is the strongest pro-embedding evidence, but it comes from a vendor-trained model on a vendor benchmark. Agent Retrieval Bench shows embeddings winning MRR. This can revisit PRINCIPLES.md later, but it is not the first fix.

## Things that contradict our current direction

- **"No code in output."** Every agent-design source returns locations plus context; our eval confirms the cost.
- **"Index only top-level declarations."** The LSP paper shows grep wins where text in strings, comments or calls matters, and that agents default to grep.
- **"No persistent index / no embeddings" as an unquestioned non-goal.** The 2608.01507 and Cursor results favor an index for question-answering workloads. The mixed grep-vs-vector evidence cuts both ways.
- **TOON as the output format.** Its own benchmark shows small, within-noise gains and weak fit for non-tabular data.
- **Planned dependents and symbols commands.** The LSP paper suggests semantic reference tools often cost more tokens than grep and agents under-use them. Prove value in the eval before building.

## Implications for monokl (prioritized)

1. **Return code, not only names.** Emit a ranked file:line hit with 1 to 3 lines of matched context, grouped by symbol. The evidence is Cognition's line-range F1 reward, Anthropic's "high-signal fields" guidance, and the LSP paper's finding that "text-enriched" results recover most of the gap. Our eval's 6x token loss to ripgrep likely comes from agents having to re-read after a name-only result. Hard evidence on snippet versus no-snippet shape is thin, so test it in our own eval.
2. **Add a text fallback over all content.** Index or scan comments, string literals, calls, routes, config and tests, not just top-level declarations. The LSP paper shows renames and literals need text matching, and Cursor and Cognition both keep grep as a core tool. Implement via `ignore` plus `grep-searcher` for a residual lexical pass, with no persistent index (consistent with PRINCIPLES). Treat declaration BM25 as a boosting signal, not the sole index.
3. **Never return silent empties.** Return a structured message with the count scanned, which terms matched zero, near-miss identifiers and a next-step hint. Evidence: Anthropic's actionable-error guidance and Agent Retrieval Bench's finding that abstention is poorly calibrated, which argues for hints over silence.
4. **Rank members above containers (or collapse them).** Score at member level and attach the parent as context. A class should not outrank the method that matches. This rests on our own eval plus Cognition's precision-favoring F-beta. No source tests it directly.
5. **Expose a concise/detailed mode and an explicit budget.** Default concise, with counts like `items_returned`/`items_total` and a truncation note that steers toward narrower queries (Anthropic, including the 25K cap). Keep it well below that cap.
6. **Make compact JSON or a plain table the default, with TOON optional.** TOON's own README shows its gains are 5 to 10% in flat cases and negative against compact JSON on nested ones. Agent-facing hits with context are not uniform tables. Benchmark on our eval before committing.
7. **Tokenize identifiers into subtokens plus the whole identifier**, with acronym handling, and index path tokens. Evidence is weak (crate practice only). Verify it ourselves with an ablation.
8. **Provide a RepoMap-style summary mode** (outline of files and exported symbols within a token budget). It was the best performer at an 8K budget in Agent Retrieval Bench, and it plays to our declaration-only strength.
9. **Keep OXC.** The TS 7 native port removes the JS compiler API but not syntactic parsing. Avoid depending on type information. If type-aware features are ever needed, the oxlint/tsgolint pattern (spawn a Go binary) is the precedent.
10. **Defer embeddings.** Cursor's +12.5% is the strongest pro-embedding evidence, but it comes from a vendor-trained model on a vendor benchmark. Agent Retrieval Bench shows embeddings winning MRR. This can revisit PRINCIPLES.md later, but it is not the first fix.

## Things that contradict our current direction

- **"No code in output."** Every agent-design source returns locations plus context; our eval confirms the cost.
- **"Index only top-level declarations."** The LSP paper shows grep wins where text in strings, comments or calls matters, and that agents default to grep.
- **"No persistent index / no embeddings" as an unquestioned non-goal.** The 2608.01507 and Cursor results favor an index for question-answering workloads. The mixed grep-vs-vector evidence cuts both ways.
- **TOON as the output format.** Its own benchmark shows small, within-noise gains and weak fit for non-tabular data.
- **Planned dependents and symbols commands.** The LSP paper suggests semantic reference tools often cost more tokens than grep and agents under-use them. Prove value in the eval before building.
